items.title: P less than 0.05 doesn't mean a result is true — or even probably true
items.claim: A study finds an effect with p = 0.04. Headlines say 'statistically significant'. The reader assumes the effect is real. In fact, in some scientific fields, more than half of 'p < 0.05' findings fail to replicate.

options.text: The probability the effect is real is 96%

The probability of seeing data at least this extreme IF the null hypothesis is true is 4%. Says nothing directly about the probability the effect is real, which requires Bayesian reasoning with priors
The result is wrong 4% of the time
P-values measure the size of effects

items.reveal_title: P-value misinterpretation and the replication crisis
items.reveal:
P-value definition: P(data at least as extreme as observed | null hypothesis true).

Common misinterpretations:
1. P is the probability the null is true (no).
2. (1 - p) is the probability the effect is real (no).
3. P measures effect size (no — small effects in large studies can have tiny p).
4. P < 0.05 means 'real effect' (no — depends on prior plausibility and study design).

Replication crisis (2010s): many influential findings in psychology, biomedicine, economics fail to replicate.
- Open Science Collaboration (2015) attempted to replicate 100 psychology studies. ~36% of replications succeeded (vs ~97% of original studies reporting significance).
- Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology (2021) attempted 23 cancer findings; only 25% of effects were as strong in replication.
- Many famous psychology results (ego depletion, power posing, money priming) have not replicated.

Causes:
- P-hacking (running many tests, reporting only significant ones).
- Publication bias (significant findings published; null results filed away).
- Small samples + multiple testing.
- Garden of forking paths (each analytic choice creates uncounted tests).
- Underpowered studies (true effects mixed with noise; significant results when found are overestimates).

Reforms: preregistration, registered reports, focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals, replication studies, statistical training reform, banishing the 0.05 threshold (some journals).

Bayesian alternatives: P(hypothesis | data) directly. Requires explicit priors but gives more interpretable answers.

The ASA's 2016 statement on p-values: don't use 'p < 0.05' as the sole basis for conclusions. Distance is being made from this old standard.
items.why: P-values look like simple measures of certainty. They aren't. Misinterpreting them has contributed to a massive scientific replication crisis. Understanding what p-values do and don't say is essential to reading research.

items.title: In London, there are at least two people with exactly the same number of hairs
items.claim: Humans have at most about 150,000 hairs on their heads. London has over 9 million people. By the pigeonhole principle, at least 60 Londoners share an EXACT hair count.

options.text: If you put more than n items into n containers, at least one container has at least 2 items; more generally, if k*n + 1 items go into n containers, some container has at least k + 1

items.reveal:
The pigeonhole principle (Dirichlet's drawer principle, 1834): if you put n + 1 objects into n boxes, at least one box has at least 2 objects.

Applied to London: ~9 million heads, at most ~150,000 possible hair counts. 9 million divided by 150,000 = 60. So at least 60 Londoners share a hair count exactly.

Elegant applications:
- In any group of 367 people, two share a birthday (366 possible birthdays + leap year).
- Among any 6 people, three are mutual friends or three mutual strangers (a Ramsey theory result, R(3,3) = 6).
- Among any 10 distinct integers from 1 to 100, two have a sum or difference divisible by 17.
- In any sequence of n squared + 1 distinct real numbers, there is a monotone subsequence of length n+1 (Erdős-Szekeres).

The principle gives existence proofs without constructing the example. It's surprisingly powerful for such a simple idea.
items.why: The pigeonhole principle looks obvious but yields non-trivial results — existence guarantees from pure counting, often where direct construction is hopeless.

items.title: Knowing the equations exactly doesn't let you predict the weather
items.claim: The atmosphere obeys Newton's laws, well-known fluid dynamics, well-known thermodynamics. Knowing all the equations doesn't let us predict beyond about 10 to 14 days. The system is deterministic but unpredictable.
items.prompt: How can determinism coexist with unpredictability?

options.text: In chaotic systems, infinitesimally different initial conditions diverge exponentially over time; predicting day 20 requires knowing today's conditions to a precision beyond physical measurement

items.reveal:
Edward Lorenz, simulating weather on a vacuum-tube computer in 1961, restarted a calculation from intermediate data printed to 3 decimal places. The internal precision was 6 places. The truncated and full simulations diverged completely within a simulated month.

He published the result in 1963 with a simplified 3-equation model showing strange attractor dynamics. His 1972 talk title — 'Does the flap of a butterfly's wings in Brazil set off a tornado in Texas?' — gave us the butterfly effect.

The key insight: any uncertainty in initial conditions doubles every few days in the atmosphere. After 10 doublings — about 2 to 3 weeks — uncertainty in tiny details has grown to dominate the whole forecast.

Ensemble weather forecasting (running many simulations from slightly perturbed starts) addresses this by giving a probability distribution rather than a single prediction.
items.why: Determinism is conflated with predictability. Lorenz showed they are different: the equations may be exact and the system may still be unpredictable in practice, because small errors grow exponentially.
